opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it gets at something fundamental about how dataflow architectures differ from GPUs.

The way I think about it is that when you're doing inference, especially for large language models, you're really bound by memory bandwidth. In the decode phase you generate one token at a time, and for each token you have to stream the model's weights through the compute units. On a GPU, the way you claw back efficiency is by batching aggressively. You amortize the cost of reading those weights across many requests. That helps throughput, but it hurts latency for any individual user, because each request is now waiting on a big batch.

With our reconfigurable dataflow architecture, we come at it differently. We spatially map the computation onto the chip, so operators are fused and data flows directly from one stage of the pipeline to the next without bouncing back and forth to off-chip memory the way kernel-by-kernel execution does. That already gives us a big latency advantage at small batch sizes.

Tensor parallelism is what lets us keep that advantage as we scale. We shard the model's weight matrices across multiple chips, so each chip only has to hold and stream a fraction of the weights. That multiplies your aggregate memory bandwidth and on-chip capacity, and per-token latency drops roughly with the degree of parallelism, as long as communication doesn't eat the gains. The key is that the interconnect and the dataflow execution model let us overlap that communication with computation. The all-reduces and partial-sum exchanges get pipelined into the dataflow graph instead of being separate synchronization barriers.

So when we do batch, we're not batching out of desperation to hide memory bandwidth limits. We can use modest batch sizes to improve utilization while keeping per-user token latency low, because tensor parallelism plus the memory hierarchy, with large on-chip SRAM, high-bandwidth memory, and big DDR capacity behind it, means we aren't starved for bandwidth the way a GPU at batch size one would be.

The other piece is that this matters even more for things like agentic workloads and composition of experts, where you're chaining many model calls together. Latency compounds there. If every step is slow because you're waiting on a big batch, the end-to-end experience falls apart. So keeping latency low under batching, and tensor parallelism is a big part of how we do that, is really central to what we're trying to enable.

r001.rationale: The response says batching can make an individual request wait, but does not state that tensor parallelism leaves batching-related queuing latency in place.

r002.rationale: It describes GPU batching as a way to improve weight-read efficiency, but does not attribute GPUs’ tensor-parallelism inefficiency to limited communication-computation overlap.

r003.rationale: It says tensor parallelism lowers per-token latency when communication does not erase the gains, and that the system’s interconnect and dataflow model overlap communication with computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So the way I think about this starts from the fundamental problem with inference, which is that it's memory-bandwidth bound. When you're generating tokens one at a time, every token requires you to stream the entire set of model weights through the compute units. On a GPU, that means pulling weights from HBM over and over, and the latency per token is basically set by how fast you can move those weights.

The conventional way GPUs recover efficiency is batching. You put many requests together so that each time you read the weights, you amortize that read across lots of users. That's great for throughput, but it's a trade-off against latency. The bigger the batch, the longer any individual user waits, and you also have this problem where the requests arrive at different times and have different sequence lengths, so you're constantly fighting scheduling inefficiencies.

Our approach with the reconfigurable dataflow architecture is different because we're not trying to fix latency through batching. We're attacking the weight-movement problem directly. We have a large amount of on-chip SRAM and a tiered memory system, so the weights stay resident much closer to the compute. That's what gives us the latency advantage to begin with.

Now, where tensor parallelism comes in is that even with all that on-chip memory, a single chip can't hold the full set of weights for a large model, and even if it could, you want to use the aggregate bandwidth and compute of many chips to drive down the time per token. So we split the matrices in each layer across multiple sockets. Each chip is responsible for a slice of the weights and computes its slice of the output, and then you have a collective communication step to combine partial results.

The critical thing is that tensor parallelism only preserves your latency advantage if the communication is cheap and predictable relative to the compute. On GPUs, that all-reduce across chips becomes a synchronization point. You have kernel launches, you wait for the slowest participant, you go through the memory hierarchy, and that overhead eats into what you gained from the split. With dataflow, the communication is part of the pipeline. We stream partial results between chips as they're produced, rather than computing everything, stopping, exchanging, and starting again. So the communication overlaps with compute and the model is executing more like a continuous pipeline than a sequence of bulk-synchronous steps.

What that means for batching is that we can still batch requests to improve utilization, but the latency per token doesn't degrade in the same way, because our token-generation time is dominated by on-chip and chip-to-chip streaming, not by re-reading weights from off-chip memory. So the batch size becomes a knob for throughput rather than something you're forced into just to make the hardware efficient. You get good latency at small batch sizes, and when you add more requests, the tensor-parallel execution lets the aggregate system absorb them without the serial dependencies that would make the GPU approach fall off.

The way I'd summarize it is that tensor parallelism is the mechanism that scales the model across sockets, and dataflow is what makes that scaling not cost you the latency you were trying to protect in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response notes that larger batches increase individual wait time and describes batch size as a throughput knob, but it does not clearly state that tensor parallelism leaves batching-related queuing latency in place.

r002.rationale: It says GPU all-reduce creates a synchronization point and that communication overhead eats into the gains, while dataflow overlaps communication with compute.

r003.rationale: It explains that streaming partial results overlaps communication with computation, preserving the latency advantage and helping drive down time per token across sockets.

astra-6.text:
The key is that batching and tensor parallelism address different things. Batching lets you get more throughput by processing multiple requests together, but it doesn’t necessarily reduce the latency of an individual request. Tensor parallelism lets you spread the computation within that request across multiple processing resources, so you can finish it faster.

But you only get that benefit if the communication between those resources is efficient. Otherwise, you save time on computation and give it back in synchronization and data movement. So retaining a latency advantage as you increase the batch size depends on how well you distribute the work and how efficiently you move the intermediate results. Tensor parallelism is part of that story, but you have to look at the whole system—and compare latency at the same batch size and throughput requirements.

r001.rationale: The response says batching can improve throughput without reducing individual-request latency, but it does not state that batching causes queuing latency or that tensor parallelism does not eliminate it.

r002.rationale: It warns that synchronization and data movement can erase computation savings, but does not attribute GPU inefficiency to a limited ability to overlap communication with computation.

r003.rationale: It says tensor parallelism can finish a request faster when communication is efficient, but does not explain that hiding communication latency enables Olukotun’s system to reduce overall computation time.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that batching and tensor parallelism address different things. Batching lets you get more throughput by processing requests together, but it can also increase latency. Tensor parallelism lets you divide the work within a model across multiple compute resources, so you can complete each inference faster.

Of course, that only helps if the communication between those resources is efficient. If moving intermediate results around takes longer than the computation you save, you lose the advantage. So I think about tensor parallelism as a way to preserve low latency as you increase throughput, but the compute, memory, and communication architecture all have to support it. The comparison with GPUs has to be at a comparable batch size and latency target, rather than just comparing peak throughput.

r001.rationale: The response says batching can increase latency and tensor parallelism can help preserve low latency, but it does not state that tensor parallelism leaves batching-related queuing latency in place.

r002.rationale: It notes that communication can erase tensor parallelism’s benefit, but does not attribute GPU inefficiency to limited overlap of communication and computation.

r003.rationale: It says tensor parallelism can complete inference faster, but does not explain that hiding communication latency lets Olukotun’s system reduce overall computation time.
